sessions.goal: Play as a brand-new player who has never heard of the game. Read the HUD and the first message, work out how to push the boulder and how to patch a module, and get as far up the hill as you can (each terrace is a release: 0.1, 0.2, ...). Note every moment of confusion, and answer the questions at the end.
sessions.verdict: The premise and the opening are strong: the first message tells you everything and shipping 0.1 feels good. But the moment the boulder rolls back (which it will, the instant you stop to patch), the game becomes a fight with the camera: I could not find which patch was the rotting module, patches landed on the wrong module as the boulder turned, and I never managed to line up behind the boulder again, so I stalled at 0.1 for 25 minutes. secondsToObjective is wall-clock (no probe); the push itself was only ~29 s of game time.
questions: In your own words, what did you think the game was about? What did the boulder, the terraces and the rot stand for?
Did the rot and the upkeep feel fair, or arbitrary? What was hardest to tell or to do?

answers.question: In your own words, what did you think the game was about? What did the boulder, the terraces and the rot stand for?
answers.answer: It is about maintaining software: the boulder is the codebase/product you keep pushing forward, each terrace is a release (version number, more users, one more module to carry), and the rot is the steady decay every module suffers (flaky tests, expiring certificates, deprecated APIs) that you must keep patching just to stay where you are. Stop pushing and it rolls back. The Sisyphus framing says the work never ends; the HUD line 'No open issues. It will not last.' sums it up.

answers.question: Did the rot and the upkeep feel fair, or arbitrary? What was hardest to tell or to do?
answers.answer: The rot rate itself felt fair and readable: one issue at a time, losing roughly 1% every few seconds, with a clear name and percentage in the HUD, and patching restored a module to 100% in 2-4 s. What felt arbitrary was the physical side: I could not tell which coloured patch was the module named in the issue, the label under the crosshair did not always match what it was over, the boulder kept rolling while I held E so the patch went to the wrong module, and once the boulder rolled back to the terrace I could not get behind it to push again. Hardest of all was re-engaging the boulder; second was finding the rotting module.

sessions.goal: Upkeep: push to the second terrace (0.2), then stay there a while and keep the boulder alive: patch modules as issues arrive (hold E), roll the boulder back from above to reach a module underneath, and retire one module (hold R). Say whether you could always tell which module was in trouble and where it was. Then push on as far as your time allows, and answer the questions at the end.
sessions.verdict: The metaphor works right away: a boulder of modules that rot as you climb, with friendly, wry text ('It will not last.'), and rolling it back to bring a face round and holding R to retire are both satisfying. Two things blocked the goal. The second push from 0.1 kept losing the boulder with no cue why, so I never reached 0.2, and nothing on the boulder marks where the rotting module sits, so finding it is a slow face-by-face hunt (side-pushing turns a new axis, but the game never says so). secondsToObjective are wall-clock seconds; there is no probe.

answers.question: In your own words, what did you think the game was about? What did the boulder, the terraces and the rot stand for?
answers.answer: It is about maintaining software: the work never ends, and every success adds to the load. The boulder is the codebase, each coloured patch a module (router, storage, parser, ui, auth, search, core). The terraces are releases: each one brings more users and a new module, which makes the boulder heavier to keep. The rot stands for dependency drift and deprecated APIs, the decay that happens to code even when nobody touches it. Retiring a module is cutting a feature: less to maintain, but some users leave.

answers.question: Did the rot and the upkeep feel fair, or arbitrary? What was hardest to tell or to do?
answers.answer: The rot felt fair and readable in the HUD: named issues with a clear cause and a percentage that falls slowly enough to plan around, worst first. The hardest part was physical, not informational. I could always tell WHICH module was in trouble, but never WHERE it was on the boulder; I had to roll it and read the crosshair prompt face by face, and rolling straight keeps showing the same faces. Pushing from the side to turn it is the trick, but I found it by accident. Hardest of all was keeping contact while pushing from 0.1 toward 0.2: the boulder kept escaping with no cue, so I never shipped 0.2.

sessions.goal: The whole climb: get the boulder to the summit (1.0), watch what happens there, follow it back down to the trailhead, and then sit (Q) and look at the view for a while. Note where the climb felt unfair, too slow or too easy, and answer the questions at the end.
sessions.verdict: The metaphor lands fast: every release adds a module, every module rots, and an untended one takes the service DOWN and users leave, all legible from the HUD. But the last terrace became a crawl (weight 8/10, ~0.27 m/s) and I stopped 14 m short of 1.0, so I never saw the summit, the roll-back or the descent; the game never tells you that rot is what makes the boulder heavy. Times are wall-clock seconds (no probe) on a heavily shared machine running ~5-14x slower than game time, so they overstate real play time.

answers.question: In your own words, what did you think the game was about? What did the boulder, the terraces and the rot stand for?
answers.answer: Maintaining software is an endless uphill push. The boulder is the codebase/product; each terrace is a release that wins users but bolts on another module, making the thing heavier. The rot is entropy in dependencies: drift, deprecated APIs, flaky tests, security advisories. Progress itself creates more upkeep, and (from the title and the 'It will not last' line) I expect the summit to undo it all, though I did not get there to see it.

answers.question: Did the rot and the upkeep feel fair, or arbitrary? What was hardest to tell or to do?
answers.answer: Mostly fair: the issues list ranks by worst, names the kind of rot, and an outage is clearly signalled. Hardest to tell: how fast each module rots and that rot (or module count) is what makes the boulder heavier, so the final slowdown felt like a wall rather than a choice. Hardest to do: reaching modules on the far/under side of the boulder to patch them while also keeping up the push; patching one module (~4 s) never kept pace with five rotting at once.

findings.title: After the boulder rolls back to a terrace, re-engaging it to push uphill is nearly impossible
findings.detail: Once the boulder had rolled back to the 0.1 terrace I spent ~15 minutes and 7+ attempts (third-person and first-person, look/strafe/walk then hold W) trying to get behind it and push it uphill again. Every 'hold w' either slid me past it onto the grass or did nothing; 'Next release 0.2: 27 m uphill' never changed. The first push from the trailhead (pre-aligned) worked perfectly, so the problem is getting lined up again: the over-the-shoulder crosshair is left of centre and is not where the character walks, and there is no cue for 'you are in pushing position'. Expected: walking into the boulder from roughly below moves it, or a visible push-contact cue.
findings.repro: pt start --profile sisyphus-strata --seed 1; pt hold w 29 (ships 0.1); pt hold w 12; pt key v; look around for ~30 s so the boulder rolls back to 0.1; then try to walk below it and pt hold w 4

findings.title: Boulder repeatedly escapes when pushing from the 0.1 terrace toward 0.2; three tries, never got past ~2 m
findings.detail: The first climb (0.0 to 0.1, about 33 m) went smoothly with hold w 5/12/15. Starting from the 0.1 terrace, I lined Sisyphus up on the trail centre with the boulder just ahead, but each push (hold w 15, hold w 6, hold w 5) lost the boulder within about 2 m. It slid off to the side and rolled back to the terrace while Sisyphus kept walking uphill alone. Nothing on screen shows that contact was lost or that he is off-centre; I only found out by turning the camera around. I expected the second push to feel like the first, or at least to get a cue such as 'it's slipping' or a lean animation. I never reached 0.2.
findings.repro: pt start --profile sisyphus-strata --seed 2; push to 0.1 (hold w ~32 s total); walk round below the boulder on the 0.1 terrace, face up the trail; pt hold w 5; pt shot; turn around: boulder back on the terrace

findings.title: Boulder silently rolls all the way back to the previous terrace with no message or indicator
findings.detail: I stopped pushing on the slope to look at modules in first-person (V). The boulder rolled back down to the 0.1 terrace out of view; 'Next release' jumped 16 m -> 28 m with no message. I could not find it for ~3 minutes (it was below the crest). This is the theme of the game so the rollback is fine, but a player needs to be told ('The boulder rolls back to 0.1') and needs a way to find it (off-screen arrow, or camera that keeps it framed).
findings.repro: pt start ...; pt hold w 29; pt hold w 12; pt key v; pt look -140 0 (several small looks, ~60 s total of commands with only short steps); pt hold w 15 -> boulder gone, 28 m

findings.title: Last terrace (0.6 -> 1.0) slows to a crawl once weight reaches 8/10 and a module is DOWN
findings.detail: Early terraces push at about 1.2 m/s (6 m per 5 s of W at 0.0; 33 m per ~30 s at 0.3). On the final 35 m terrace, with 12 modules, weight 8/10 and search DOWN, 22 s of holding W moved the boulder only 6 m (20 -> 14 m). I ran out of time 14 m short of 1.0. Nothing on screen explains what weight is made of or that patching/retiring would lighten it, so a player who just pushes hits a wall without knowing which lever to pull. Expected either a visible hint (e.g. 'rotting modules make it heavier') or a gentler curve.
findings.repro: pt start --profile sisyphus-strata --seed 3; pt hold w 5; pt hold Shift_L+w 10; pt hold w 13; pt hold w 30; pt hold w 32; pt hold w 3; (patch ui) pt hold e 4.5; pt hold w 30; pt hold w 36; pt hold w 38; pt hold w 8; pt hold w 2.5; pt hold w 25; pt hold w 22; pt shot slow

findings.title: No way to see WHERE on the boulder the rotting module is; the HUD names it but the boulder does not mark it
findings.detail: The HUD lists open issues by name (router, storage, parser). The only way to locate one is to roll the boulder and read the crosshair prompt face by face. Rolling straight back keeps the same great circle, so the same faces come round again: ui stayed under the crosshair for 6+ nudges. Finding parser took about 10 minutes. It only came into reach when I pushed the boulder sideways along the terrace from its side, which nothing in the game teaches. The rotting faces have no colour, glow or marker. So: I could always tell WHICH module was in trouble, but never WHERE it was.
findings.repro: pt start ... --seed 2; reach 0.1; let parser rot; stand above the boulder; repeat (pt hold w 0.4; pt wait 0.4; pt shot) and read the prompt

findings.title: No way to tell which coloured patch of the boulder is the module named in an open issue
findings.detail: The HUD lists 'search  flaky test 93%' but the boulder is several large patches in similar dark colours (very dark in shadow) and nothing ties a colour to a name. The only way is to sweep the crosshair across the boulder and read the label. Finding 'search' took ~4 minutes of full-circle camera sweeps; the module was apparently underneath. Expected: the rotting module glows/pulses (I saw a faint yellow glow once on auth, but not consistently), or the issue line shows its colour swatch.
findings.repro: pt start ...; pt hold w 29; pt hold w 15 -> 'search flaky test' issue; try to find 'search' on the boulder

findings.title: 'Patching [###...]' bar stays on screen after releasing E and does not track module health
findings.detail: After patching auth the module read 'healthy (100%)' within ~2 s but the bar kept filling; after release, 'Patching [######......]' stayed under every label for minutes (including over other modules), instead of reverting to 'Hold E to patch'. I could not tell when a patch was done.
findings.repro: pt hold e 2 on a rotting module; release; pt look around; pt shot
alsoTitled: Patch prompt keeps showing a stale 'Patching [####...]' bar after the module is healthy and E is released
Patch/retire progress bar stays on screen after the key is released, attached to the next (healthy) module

findings.title: 'Hold E to patch' is offered mid-slope, but stopping to patch lets the boulder roll back down
findings.detail: 9 m short of 0.2 the prompt said 'router: dependency drift ... Hold E to patch'. I held E, and the boulder rolled back down the slope to the 0.1 terrace (next release 9 m -> 28 m), so the patch never happened. Either the prompt should be hidden on the slope or there should be a warning; the opening text never says you can only patch on a terrace.
findings.repro: push to within ~10 m of 0.2 with an open issue under the crosshair; pt hold e 2; pt shot

findings.title: Boulder keeps rolling while you patch, so the hold-E lands on the wrong module
findings.detail: Aimed at 'search' (n0) and held E 3 s; the boulder rotated under the crosshair and the progress went to 'ui' instead. search stayed at 57%. Patching on a slope means fighting the roll.
findings.repro: with the boulder near the bottom of a slope, aim at an unhealthy module, pt hold e 3

findings.title: Crosshair module label does not match what the crosshair is visually over
findings.detail: Several times the label under the crosshair named a module while the crosshair was visibly over sky/ground beside the boulder (e.g. 'search: flaky test' with the crosshair on the village background), and when I then held E the patch went to a different module ('ui', already healthy) because the boulder had moved. Labels also seemed to lag one look behind. Expected: the label reflects exactly the surface under the crosshair this frame.
findings.repro: pt start ...; after 0.1 with boulder on the terrace, pt key v; pt look 300 0 repeatedly, pt step 2, pt shot each time

findings.title: Rot backlog outpaces patching while pushing; no guidance on when to stop and patch
findings.detail: By 0.5 five modules were rotting at once (13-64%). A patch takes ~4 s held and needs the module under the crosshair; modules under the boulder need it rolled back. With continuous pushing, the backlog only grows and the first module hits 0% shortly after 0.6. The HUD lists issues clearly, but there is no sense of how fast each rots, so it is hard to plan which to patch.
findings.repro: As above up to 0.5; pt shot rotpile

findings.title: Help bar lists 'F5 save  F9 load' in a driven session where they do nothing
findings.detail: The controls strip shows F5 save / F9 load, but in a driven session they do nothing. Minor, but the help should match what works.
findings.repro: pt start ...; pt hold w 5; pt shot (help strip at bottom)
alsoTitled: Help bar advertises F5 save / F9 load in a driven session where they do nothing

findings.title: Floating terrace labels '0.2'/'0.3' render through the boulder and over the prompt text
findings.detail: In first-person (V) the world-space version labels draw on top of the boulder and collide with the crosshair prompt, producing garbled text like 'pa0s2r' and 'patch0.3'.
findings.repro: pt start ...; pt hold w 29; pt hold w 12; pt key v; pt look 0 -80; pt shot

findings.title: Mouse pitch feels inverted / inconsistent and yaw scale differs between views
findings.detail: pt look 0 +60 tilted the view up in third-person and pt look 0 -80 looked down, the opposite of the harness convention (+ down). A 600 px yaw was ~180 degrees one time and ~90 another, which made 'turn around' guesswork.
findings.repro: pt look 0 60; pt step 2; pt shot; compare with pt look 0 -60

findings.title: Opening message and first push are excellent
findings.detail: Positive: the first screen explains everything in three lines ('The boulder is your software. Push it up to the next terrace to ship a release (W, into it). Every release adds a module, and every module rots. Hold E on one to patch it.'), and 'No open issues. It will not last.' sets the tone. Shipping 0.1 ('Shipped 0.1. New module: search.', users 10 -> 50) felt great. Note the full controls bar only appeared after shipping 0.1, not at the start.
findings.repro: pt start ...; pt shot start; pt hold w 29; pt shot

findings.title: Outage feedback is clear and well done (positive)
findings.detail: When search hit 0% it shows DOWN in red, HUD line 2 turns red 'OUTAGE: users are leaving' and users drop 400 -> 349 -> 280. Consequence is legible immediately. Version jump 0.6 -> 1.0 on the next terrace was a nice surprise ('Next release 1.0: 35 m uphill').
findings.repro: Continue pushing past 0.6 without patching; pt shot outage

findings.title: Rolling-back and retire feedback is good (positive)
findings.detail: 'Rolling it back to turn it' appears as soon as you push from above. Retiring shows 'Retired. One less thing to keep, and a few users miss it.' with Modules 7->6 and Users 50->46, which makes the trade-off clear. 'No open issues. It will not last.' sets the tone well.
findings.repro: on a terrace, from above: pt hold w 1; then pt hold r 4 on a module

findings.title: Sit (Q) is a lovely beat (positive)
findings.detail: Q hides the HUD, pulls the camera out to the view up the hill, caption 'The boulder is still. For a moment, so are you.' The boulder holds still on the slope.
findings.repro: Mid-climb: pt key q; pt wait 3; pt shot sit

findings.title: World-space terrace sign label ('0.1') draws on top of the HUD issue percentages
findings.detail: On the 0.1 terrace the yellow '0.1' marker label overlaps the open-issue percentage column in the HUD, which makes the numbers hard to read (for example '0.1' over '65%'). The HUD should draw above world labels or keep clear of them.
findings.repro: stand on the 0.1 terrace facing downhill toward the sign; pt shot
